summary: Since April 1, 2025 Namibia requires a visa from nationals of countries that have not reciprocated its visa exemption — including most EU states, the US, UK, Canada and Japan, which can get it on arrival or online in advance for NAD 1,600 (NAD 1,200 for African Union nationals); nationalities not on the visa-on-arrival list must obtain a visa before travel. Citizens of the countries on the Ministry of Home Affairs' exemption list, including most SADC states, need no visa for holidays.

safety.text: Muggers often target tourists in Windhoek, and attacks can be violent, at any time of day and in busy city-centre areas. Theft from vehicles is common, particularly at service stations. Accidents are common on gravel and dirt roads: in the January–April rainy season keep below 80 km/h on gravel, carry two spare tyres and plenty of water, and avoid driving at night outside towns, where wildlife and livestock are serious hazards.

tips.text: The UK government's travel advice says accidents are common on gravel and dirt roads and that many gravel roads deteriorate in the rainy season (January to April). For that season it advises not going faster than 80 km/h, carrying 2 spare tyres and avoiding driving at night outside towns, where wildlife and livestock are serious hazards.

Namibia's entry rules changed on April 1, 2025: nationals of countries that have not reciprocated Namibia's visa exemption, including EU states, the US, UK, Canada and Japan, now pay NAD 1,600 per adult for a visa on arrival or e-visa.

The UK government's travel advice says Namibian immigration officials will not accept an abridged birth certificate: children aged 17 and under need a full one with both parents' details, plus an affidavit of consent from any parent or guardian who is not travelling.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Namibia?
faq.answer: Since April 1, 2025, nationals of countries that have not reciprocated Namibia's visa exemption — including most EU states, the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Japan — must obtain a visa, available on arrival or online in advance for NAD 1,600 per adult (NAD 1,200 for African Union nationals). Nationalities not on the visa-on-arrival list must get a visa before travelling. Citizens of the countries on the Ministry of Home Affairs' exemption list, including most SADC states, need no visa for holidays.

faq.question: How does Namibia's visa on arrival work?
faq.answer: Eligible nationals apply at a port of entry, pay NAD 1,600 per adult (NAD 1,200 for African Union nationals; NAD 800 or 600 for children aged 6–11, free under 6) by card, and receive a multiple-entry visa for the period requested, up to 90 days. They can also apply in advance as an e-visa through the Ministry of Home Affairs eServices portal, which the Ministry calls the preferred option.

faq.question: Who can still enter Namibia visa-free?
faq.answer: The Ministry of Home Affairs fact sheet lists, among others, Angola, Botswana, Brazil, Cuba, Eswatini, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Jamaica, Kenya, Lesotho, Macau, Malawi, Malaysia, Mauritius, Mozambique, Russia, Seychelles, Singapore, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe as countries whose nationals do not require visas for holidays. No official source we could read states the length of stay.

faq.question: Do children need extra documents to enter Namibia?
faq.answer: Yes. The UK government's travel advice says children aged 17 and under must carry a valid passport and a full (unabridged) birth certificate with both parents' details; if a child travels with one parent, the other should give consent in an affidavit. Canada's advice also requires a long-form birth certificate and proof of consent.

faq.question: What should I know before driving in Namibia?
faq.answer: Canada's travel advice says road conditions are generally good, but most roads outside urban areas are gravel, and fatal accidents — often linked to excessive speed on gravel — are common, many involving a single tourist vehicle. It advises avoiding night-time driving outside urban centres and notes that roadside assistance is unreliable or non-existent outside Windhoek.
